explanation: Heels reached Europe partly through Persian riding boots. Louis XIV of France wore red heels and restricted them to his court, and women wore heels too.

claims.text: In 17th-century Europe, high heels were fashionable among wealthy and aristocratic men.
Heeled shoes reached Europe partly through the influence of Persian riding footwear.
Louis XIV wore red-heeled shoes and restricted red heels to members of his court.
Women in 17th-century Europe also wore high heels.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Aristocratic men: Heels signaled rank for men. Men wore them to imply their upper-class status, and in 17th century France, heels were exclusively worn by aristocrats.

claimResults.note: Results are Wikipedia, Britannica and the Bata Shoe Museum, so the call counts at Tier B at worst. The summary's disagreements (Louis XIII or XIV, late 16th or early 17th century arrival) do not touch this claim.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Persian origin: Heels likely began as functional riding gear. One source says Persian cavalry wore galesh, a kind of boot with heels, to ensure their feet stayed in the stirrups starting in the 10th century. The Bata Shoe Museum says Europeans adopted it at end of the 16th century, while Wikipedia dates the arrival in Europe to the early 17th century.

claimResults.note: Standard claim. Sources differ on when heels reached Europe, not on the Persian riding origin.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Louis XIV and red heels: Sources agree he made red heels a status marker, though they differ on who started it. One Wikipedia article says his predecessor King Louis XIII introduced the red heel to the court of French nobility. Britannica says Louis XIV (1638-1715) liked his heels painted red, and others were allowed to emulate his striking style only with his Majesty's permission.

claimResults.note: Standard claim. Sources differ on who started the red heel, which the claim does not say; Britannica states Louis XIV wore red heels and controlled who could copy them.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Women: Your premise that women adopted heels is supported, but later. One source says the trend spread to women's fashion toward the end of the 17th century. By the mid-17th century, men's and women's heels already differed: men's fashion increasingly favoured the sturdy 'Polony' heel made of stacked leather, while women's shoes tended feature heels made of leather-covered wood whittled into more sinuous shapes.

claimResults.note: Women wore heels by the mid to late 17th century, which is what the claim says.
